/compare/seedance-vs-wan.question: Seedance vs Wan: which AI video model should you use?
/compare/seedance-vs-wan.verdict: Pick Seedance 2 when the clip ships: it renders 720p or 1080p with synchronized audio and strong prompt following from about $1.28 per 5s. Pick Wan when volume matters more than polish: at roughly half the price (from 90 credits, about $0.90 per 5s), it is the workhorse for drafts and social content, but it is silent and tops out at 720p.

/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.title: Pose to Witch: Six New Ways to Control AI Video
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.excerpt: Turn ordinary footage into a pose, depth, edge, line, or masked control signal, then regenerate it as a new character or world. We shipped six MiniMax H3 control-video tools and tested the full path with a real pose-to-witch render.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.0.text: Video-to-video usually asks one model to preserve everything and change everything at once. That is why a strong style transfer can lose the walk, flatten the camera move, or slowly replace the performer with a different person. Our new H3 control tools split the problem in two: first extract the part of the source clip that matters, then use that signal to guide a new generation.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.1.text: We have launched six focused workflows—Canny, Depth, HED, MLSD, Pose, and Video Inpainting—on the MiniMax-H3-Fun ControlNet Union model. Each tool accepts a normal source video. ManifoldGen prepares the correct control pass automatically, or you can turn preprocessing off and upload a control video you prepared elsewhere.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.2.text: The test: turn a performance into a forest witch
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.3.text: For the launch test, we used a short pose-driving clip and asked for a full-body forest witch in layered emerald robes, silver hair, and a moonlit ancient forest. The output keeps the source performance and hand timing while replacing the person, wardrobe, lighting, and location.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.4.example.label: Real launch render — Pose control
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.4.example.note: This is the actual production output, not a concept mockup. Pose control carries the body performance; the prompt controls the new subject and world.

/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.8.text: The useful distinction is what you cannot afford to lose. Choose Pose when the performance is sacred, Depth when the camera and volume matter, Canny for bold shape, HED for nuanced contour, and MLSD for constructed geometry. Use Inpainting when most of the frame is already right and only one region should change.

/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.11.text: You do not need to run OpenPose, a depth estimator, or an edge detector before uploading. Keep “Extract control from my normal video” enabled and the worker derives a temporally aligned control video before generation. Advanced users can disable that switch to send an already prepared Canny, Depth, HED, MLSD, or Pose pass directly.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.12.title: Inpainting needs one extra file
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.12.text: Upload the source clip and a matching mask video. White areas are regenerated through time; black areas stay anchored to the original. A stable mask produces a more stable edit.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.14.items.0: Control strength decides how strictly the new shot follows the guide. Start near the default; lower it for a larger creative change and raise it when motion or geometry begins to drift.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.14.items.1: Prompt the replacement, not the source. Describe the new subject, wardrobe, environment, light, materials, and desired finish.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.14.items.2: Use a seed when comparing prompts or strength values. Keeping it fixed makes the effect of one changed setting easier to judge.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.14.items.3: Start at 480p on a short excerpt. Once motion and framing work, move to 576p or 720p and render the longer clip.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.15.text: The launch tools accept clips up to 15 seconds, with 3, 5, 8, 10, and 15-second output choices. Resolutions are 480p, 576p, and 720p. Generation runs as a durable asynchronous job, so a long render does not depend on keeping one browser request open.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.17.text: Before you generate, the page shows an estimate based on duration and resolution. At launch, the approximate 480p prices are $1.16 for 3 seconds, $1.44 for 5 seconds, $1.88 for 8 seconds, and $2.88 for 15 seconds. A 576p render is about 1.35× the 480p estimate and 720p is about 2×. The final charge settles from actual GPU runtime, so you pay for the compute used rather than a padded fixed ceiling.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.18.title: Prototype short, finish high
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.18.text: Control-video generation is high-memory GPU work. Test the prompt and control strength on the shortest useful section at 480p, then spend on the final duration and resolution after the motion is right.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.20.text: These six tools use the MiniMax H3 Community License. They are currently unavailable in the United States, European Union, United Kingdom, and South Korea. The tool checks territory before generation and requires license acceptance in the interface. If the tool is available where you are, review the linked model license for the restrictions that apply to your use.
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.21.items.0.label: Read the model license
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.21.items.1.label: Open Pose Video
/blog/h3-control-video-style-transfer.blocks.23.text: Start with a clean, readable performance: one person walking, dancing, casting, or turning in frame. Run it through Pose and describe a character whose silhouette can plausibly follow that motion—a witch, armored knight, forest spirit, or stylized creature. Then take the same source through Depth or HED. Seeing which information each control preserves is the fastest way to understand the six tools, and often reveals a stronger treatment than the one you planned.

/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.title: We Made Two Short Films With Dialogue Using One Video Model
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.excerpt: Two complete short films — a magic-noir tragedy and a stranded-crew sci-fi story — made with 16 structured H3 prompts: one verbatim IDENTITY LOCK per shot for character consistency, dialogue written into the prompt for generation-time lip-sync, and music mixed in afterwards. The workflow, prompts, and render numbers.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.0.text: We made two complete short films with dialogue — Ember, a magic-noir tragedy set in a desert city, and Hollow Orbit, the story of a crashed survey ship on a bioluminescent tidally-locked planet — using nothing but our H3 video model on our own GPU stack. Each film is 8 shots × 5 seconds: 16 shots total, and every shot is a single structured prompt. H3 has no memory between shots, so character consistency lives in the prompt itself, and dialogue is generated by the model, with lip-sync happening in generation. This article is the whole workflow: the identity technique, the dialogue format, why music never enters the model, and what the renders cost.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.2.text: Both films were planned as shot lists first and prompts second — one prompt per shot, rendered sequentially on one local GPU worker. Ember is a magic-noir tragedy: a street sorceress steals a forbidden ember to save her dying brother, the guard who loves her takes a killing bolt for her, and she burns her own spark to save him, scattering into embers at sunrise. Strife, love, loss — forty seconds of it. Hollow Orbit strands a survey ship on a tidally-locked planet: the alien Choir rebuilds their engine but demands a resident mind, co-pilot Lena chooses to stay and becomes the helm, and the valley blooms in her tattoo geometry as the ship escapes.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.3.example.label: Film 1 — Ember
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.3.example.note: Shot 1 establishes geography and the theft in one prompt. The IDENTITY LOCK pins Sera while everything underneath it — location, action, camera, light, audio — is new per shot; the remaining seven prompts change only those variables.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.3.example.media.0.caption: Ember — 8 shots × 5 seconds, generated and cut end to end
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.4.example.label: Film 2 — Hollow Orbit
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.4.example.note: The whole film is eight such prompts. The ship, the valley, and the Choir reappear across shots because their descriptors repeat verbatim — the same discipline the IDENTITY LOCK applies to faces.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.4.example.media.0.caption: Hollow Orbit — 8 shots × 5 seconds, dialogue generated by the model
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.6.text: Each H3 generation is independent: shot 7 has no knowledge of shot 6. Consistency is therefore a prompt discipline, not a model feature. Every shot prompt opens with the same IDENTITY LOCK block, pasted verbatim, that pins everything about a character that must never change. Here is the truncated SERA lock from Ember's spec:
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.8.text: The lock fixes face, hair, wardrobe, jewelry, even how her magic manifests — and it is pasted into all eight of Ember's prompts without changing a word. The shot prompt underneath changes only what should change: location, action, camera, light, sound. Drift starts the moment you reword the lock; a "black braided crown" that becomes "loose beach waves" in shot 6 is a different character.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.10.text: Lines are written into the shot prompt with their exact wording, and H3 performs them — lip-sync happens during generation, not in a post pass. Two rules hold every dialogue shot together: name the speaker, and mark the words as fixed. Ember's last line to the guard, as she burns her spark at dawn:
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.12.text: And Hollow Orbit's decision beat, once the Choir has rebuilt the engine and named its price:
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.14.text: Both lines are short on purpose: a close-up, one clause, the exact words in quotes, and an Audio: line carrying voice and diegetic sound only. The "no score" instruction is not decoration — it is what makes the next section possible.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.15.text: Music stays out of the model
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.16.text: H3 renders dialogue, ambience, and effects in generation, which means a score baked into the same pass would fight the dialogue track inside the model's own audio. We keep music out entirely and treat it as a mix problem.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.17.title: Score in post, not in the prompt
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.17.text: Instrumental beds are generated separately with our music model and mixed under the dialogue in ffmpeg, sidechain-ducked so the bed dips whenever a character speaks. Every Audio: line in a shot prompt lists diegetic sound only — voices, wind, hull hum. Music never enters generation.
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.19.rows.0.1: 16 shots — 8 per film, 5 seconds each, one structured prompt per shot
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.19.rows.1.1: Our own GPU stack: one local GPU worker, shots rendered sequentially
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.19.rows.3.1: IDENTITY LOCK block repeated verbatim in every prompt
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.19.rows.4.1: Written into the prompt with exact wording, generated and lip-synced by H3
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.19.rows.5.1: Instrumental beds from our music model, mixed under dialogue in ffmpeg
/blog/h3-short-films-ember-hollow-orbit.blocks.20.text: The same stack is open in the studio: direct shots at /studio, score them with the generator at /tools/music-generator, and keep every asset searchable on this site. Write one IDENTITY LOCK, paste it into every prompt verbatim, put the exact spoken words in quotes, and keep music out of the model — that is the entire method behind both films.

/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.title: Seedance 2 vs Kling 3.0 vs Veo 3.1: pick the flagship that fits
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.excerpt: Three flagship video models on one API: cinematic all-rounder, audio-first multi-shot scenes, and photoreal physical motion. Prices, audio, and the shots each one wins.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.0.text: ManifoldGen now serves three flagship video families side by side: Seedance 2 (ByteDance), Kling 3.0 (Kuaishou), and Veo 3.1 (Google). Each has a different center of gravity — cinematic character work, multi-shot scenes with audio, and photoreal physical motion. They share one API key and one prepaid credit balance, so the question is not which platform to use but which model should run which shot.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.2.items.0: Seedance 2 — the cinematic all-rounder: strongest prompt fidelity and character coherence, 1080p with synced audio, reference-guided variants. From ~$1.67 per 5s at full quality.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.2.items.1: Kling 3.0 — native audio at a lower entry price: Standard from 76 credits (~$0.76), Pro adds 1080p and improved lipsync from 101 credits, 2.6 lane for volume.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.2.items.2: Veo 3.1 — the photoreal flagship: believable physics and synchronized sound from 240 credits (~$2.40), with Veo 3.1 Fast at 90 credits when a still needs realistic motion on a budget.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.5.text: All prices are measured on ManifoldGen and bill from the same credit balance: 1 credit = $0.01. Run the same prompt through all three in one session and pay only for what generates.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.8.text: Seedance keeps characters coherent through multi-subject action and follows complex prompts better than the other two. For dialogue scenes, brand work, or any clip where a person must stay the same person from first frame to last, it is the default. The reference variants (Seedance 2.5 Reference, Seedance 2 Reference) lock a character, set, or palette across a full take.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.9.text: Multi-shot scenes and budget audio → Kling 3.0
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.10.text: Kling is tuned for scenes that cut: multi-shot structure, filmic camera moves, and synced audio at a lower entry price than Seedance full quality. Pro adds 1080p and notably better lipsync, which makes it the value pick for talking-head style clips. The 2.6 lane costs even less for high-volume work that still needs sound.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.11.text: Photoreal stills and physics-heavy motion → Veo 3.1
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.12.text: When the output must read as real footage — water, fabric, faces, product physics — Veo 3.1 is the most believable of the three. It is image-to-video first, and its Fast lane animates a still with realistic motion and synced audio for about a third of the flagship price.
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.13.title: The workflow that actually uses all three
/blog/seedance-vs-kling-vs-veo.blocks.13.text: Draft the edit with LTX 2 ($0.09), move to Kling for budget audio cuts, then finish hero shots with Seedance or Veo. One key, one balance, zero migration.

/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.title: Best AI video model for anime: Wan, Happy Horse, Kling and the honest breakdown
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.excerpt: Which served model actually produces anime that looks like anime? Wan for style and budget, Happy Horse for expressive character animation, Kling for audio and multi-shot scenes.
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.0.text: ManifoldGen serves several models that can produce anime-style footage, but they fail differently. Wan is the safe all-rounder for illustration styles at a low price. Happy Horse is built for expressive stylized character motion. Kling 3.0 adds native audio and multi-shot scenes. Seedance handles sakuga-style action when characters must stay coherent through fast cuts. This guide maps each one to the anime jobs it actually wins.
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.2.rows.0.2: Broad illustration styles and camera-move prompting at ~$0.90 per 5s
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.2.rows.1.2: Purpose-built for lively, exaggerated motion from 168 credits (~$1.68)
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.2.rows.2.2: Synced sound and filmic cuts from 76 credits (~$0.76)
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.2.rows.3.2: Character coherence through fast action at 1080p, ~$1.67 per 5s
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.4.text: Wan handles a wide berth of illustration styles — cel shading, painterly, watercolor, mecha detail — and responds well to camera-move prompting like pan, tilt, and push-in. It is silent and caps at 720p, which is fine for drafts, style tests, and volume content. At 90 credits (~$0.90) per 5-second clip it makes full-episode coverage affordable in a way no premium model does.
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.6.text: Happy Horse: expressive animation from a still
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.7.text: Happy Horse animates a still image with lively, characterful motion. It is tuned for stylized characters and playful scenes — dance-like movement, exaggerated reactions, meme-ready energy. It is image-input only: feed it a character sheet or a single clean illustration and it brings the pose to life. The tradeoff is the same as Wan: 720p, no audio, and energy over realism.
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.8.title: Character consistency trick
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.8.text: Generate the character once in the image model that nails your design (try /tools/h3-image or /tools/nano-banana), then feed that still into Happy Horse instead of prompting a new character every time.
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.10.text: Kling 3.0 is the value pick when the clip needs sound: Standard text-to-video starts at 76 credits (~$0.76) with synced audio, and Pro adds 1080p and better lipsync from 101 credits. Multi-shot prompting — "cut from the close-up to the wide reaction" — is a Kling strength, which helps for short anime segments that should feel directed rather than single-take.
/blog/best-ai-video-model-for-anime.blocks.12.text: When the cut is fast and characters must stay coherent through action — a fight, a chase, a transformation — Seedance 2 is the strongest of the four at 1080p with native audio. It costs the most, so the practical pattern is: Wan drafts, Kling middle tier, Seedance for the two or three shots an audience will actually scrutinize.

/blog/ai-video-api-cost-guide-2026.blocks.5.items.1: Move to the audio lane for story beats: Kling 3.0 and Seedance give synced audio without a separate sound pass, so one render is the whole cut.
/blog/ai-video-api-cost-guide-2026.blocks.5.items.2: Reserve the flagship for hero frames: Veo 3.1 at $0.40/s only where the shot must look physical.
/blog/ai-video-api-cost-guide-2026.blocks.5.items.3: Use one key: every lane above bills from the same prepaid balance, so switching models mid-project is a parameter change, not an integration change.
/blog/ai-video-api-cost-guide-2026.blocks.7.text: A 30-second product ad, 12 shots: draft all 12 in LTX 2 (~$1.10), move the 4 hero shots to Seedance 2 full quality (~$2.70), keep one Veo 3.1 photoreal insert (~$1.20). Total under $6 before music — and the music track itself is $0.35 flat on the same balance. The API surface for this is one POST per shot; the per-model tool pages carry the exact request shapes.

/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.title: How to Use Kling 3.0 for Cinematic AI Video
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.excerpt: Kling 3.0 turns prompts and stills into multi-shot cinematic clips with native synced audio. Here is how to prompt it, which tier to pick, and what each setting costs.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.0.text: Kling 3.0 is the strongest Kling release for narrative work: it plans multiple shots inside one generation, keeps characters consistent across them, and ships native synced audio — dialogue, ambience, and effects — without a post pass. On ManifoldGen it runs in two tiers (Standard and Pro) with text-to-video and image-to-video routes for each. This guide covers when each tier earns its price, how to prompt for multi-shot scenes, and the settings that actually change the output.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.2.text: Pick the tier by job, not by pride
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.3.items.0: Standard is the drafting tier. Same motion engine at 720p; use it for story beats, shot lists, and anything you will recut anyway.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.3.items.1: Pro buys 1080p output and noticeably better lipsync and face fidelity under speech. Use it for the shots that survive the edit.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.3.items.2: Image to Video is the identity lock. When a character must look exactly right, generate the still first (any image model), then animate it instead of rolling dice on text-to-video.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.5.text: Kling 3.0's signature trick is generating several coherent shots in one clip. It follows numbered shot structure far better than prose:
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.7.text: Three rules make this reliable. Number the shots so the model cannot blur their boundaries. Give each shot its own camera distance (wide / close-up / medium) rather than one global camera move. And specify audio as its own line — Kling generates the soundtrack, so tell it what world should sound like.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.9.text: For spoken lines, put the words in quotes inside the shot they belong to and keep sentences short: "We hold until dawn," she says into the wind. Lipsync quality scales with face size in frame — dialogue belongs in close-ups, not wides. If a line fights the clip length, cut the words before you cut the seconds; rushed speech reads as artifact.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.10.title: Audio is generated, not added
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.10.text: Kling 3.0 always renders its own soundtrack. Describe the sound scene (wind, room tone, music style) the same way you describe the visual one, or you will get generic ambience over a specific picture.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.12.items.0: Shots melt into each other — your shot descriptions share actions. One subject, one action, one camera per shot.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.12.items.1: Faces drift across shots — switch that character to Image to Video from a locked still.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.12.items.2: Lipsync misses — bring the speaker closer to camera and shorten the line to under eight words.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.12.items.3: Ten seconds feel cramped — split into two five-second generations at different camera distances and cut them together; it reads as intentional coverage.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.12.items.4: 1080p requested but soft — source prompt detail, not upscale, drives perceived sharpness. Add lens and lighting specifics.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-3.blocks.13.text: Open the workflow at /tools/kling-3 for Standard drafts, /tools/kling-3-pro for finals, and /tools/kling-3-image for stills you need to keep — the API mirror of each lives at /api/video-generators/kling-3 and friends.

/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.title: How to Use Kling 2.6 When Budget Matters
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.excerpt: Kling 2.6 Pro is the value tier of the Kling line: reliable motion, native audio, and 1080p at roughly two-thirds of Kling 3.0 pricing. Here is where it wins and how to prompt it.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.0.text: Not every shot needs the flagship. Kling 2.6 Pro is the previous-generation tier fal still serves because it earns its keep: dependable single-subject motion, native synced audio, and 1080p output at 14 credits a second — about two-thirds of Kling 3.0 Pro's rate. For social cuts, product loops, and animating stills on a budget, it is frequently indistinguishable in the final edit.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.3.items.0: Single-subject action — one person, one animal, one product. 2.6 holds identity well when nothing competes for the frame.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.3.items.1: Loops and ambient b-roll — rain, traffic, firelight, waves. Repetitive natural motion is where the older engine shows no age.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.3.items.2: Volume drafts — ten variants of one concept cost less here than three rounds on the flagship.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.3.items.3: Stylized content — illustration, anime, claymation looks hide model generations better than photoreal humans do.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.5.text: Kling 2.6 is a one-shot generator, not a multi-shot planner like 3.0. Give it a single continuous take with one camera idea:
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.7.text: The anatomy: one camera move (dolly-in), one subject action (pouring), two or three ambient clauses (steam, light, sway), then an audio line naming the room. That is enough. Stacking five actions makes any model improvise; 2.6 simply picks one at random.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.9.text: The image-to-video route is the quiet bargain here. Compose the frame in an image model where retakes are nearly free, then hand the still to Kling 2.6 with motion-only language: breeze, blink, pour, flicker. Never re-describe the scene in the video prompt — the image already decided it, and conflicting words cause warping.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.10.title: Spend the savings on takes
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.10.text: The pro workflow is not a better model — it is more rolls. Two 2.6 passes with different seeds beat one 3.0 pass you cannot afford to repeat.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.12.items.0: Hands mangle during detailed work — cut away before the fingers act or move the action offscreen with sound carrying it.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.12.items.1: Audio ignores your style note — name instruments and room materials ("felt-piano, tiled walls"), not moods.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.12.items.2: Motion stalls mid-clip — the prompt described a state, not a process. Replace "a cup on the table" with "coffee being poured".
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.12.items.3: Text artifacts crawl into signage — ask for blank signs or add "no readable text" to the prompt.
/blog/how-to-use-kling-2-6.blocks.13.text: Try it at /tools/kling-26 or animate from a still at /tools/kling-26-image; both are mirrored for automation at /api/video-generators/kling-26.

/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.title: How to Use Veo 3.1 for Photoreal Video With Sound
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.excerpt: Google's Veo 3.1 is the photorealism benchmark: physics that hold, native dialogue, and 4/6/8-second takes with synced audio. Fast covers drafts at 90 credits; Standard covers finals.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.0.text: Veo 3.1 is the model you reach for when the clip must look filmed rather than generated: real-world physics, believable skin and water, and the best native dialogue in the field. On ManifoldGen it runs as image-to-video in two tiers — Fast for iteration, Standard for finals — both with synchronized sound.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.3.text: Both ManifoldGen routes are image-to-video, and that is the correct workflow anyway. Veo follows composition religiously, so a still gives you casting, framing, and lighting direction for free — then the video prompt only has to describe motion and sound. Generate your frame with any image model, pick the take you would have shot, and animate it.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.4.text: Write motion like a director, not a caption
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.6.items.0: One subject action per clause — "turns", "wipes", "looks" are three beats Veo will sequence faithfully.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.6.items.1: State the camera explicitly — "static", "slow push-in". Silence invites drift.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.6.items.2: Name what should not move — "depth of field stays on her hands" pins focus better than hoping.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.6.items.3: Score it — ambience, one music cue, or a weather layer. Unspecified audio defaults to room tone.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.8.text: Veo renders speech with lip alignment and even accent control if you name it. Keep lines under twelve words, put them in quotes, and attribute them: He says, "Lock the door behind you." Faces read best at medium close-up or tighter; dialogue in a wide shot wastes the feature.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.9.title: Fast is the look-dev tier
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.9.text: Prompt structure transfers one-to-one between tiers. Lock motion and timing on Fast at 90 credits per pass, then re-run the identical request on Standard only for the shots that made the cut.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.11.text: Four seconds suits inserts and social loops; six handles a full action beat; eight fits a line of dialogue plus a reaction. If a scene needs more, generate two eight-second takes with matched stills (same character frame, different camera) and cut — Veo keeps identity across cuts far better than across a single long generation.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.13.items.0: Physics show off — water, cloth, and fire are Veo strengths, but they need space. Tight frames force shortcuts; widen the shot instead of slowing the motion.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.13.items.1: Subject ignores the source image — your prompt re-describes appearance. Strip adjectives about the person; keep only motion and audio.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.13.items.2: Dialogue sounds dubbed — shorten the line and mark delivery ("quietly", "over the shoulder").
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.13.items.3: Eight seconds sag in the middle — add one sustained ambient clause (rain continues, crowd murmur persists) to carry the middle beat.
/blog/how-to-use-veo-3-1.blocks.14.text: Run it at /tools/veo-3-1-fast for drafts and /tools/veo-3-1 for finals; automation mirrors live at /api/video-generators/veo-3-1-fast and /api/video-generators/veo-3-1.

/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.title: How to Use Seedance 2.5 for Long Single-Take Video
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.excerpt: Seedance 2.5 plans a whole shot at once: coherent single takes up to 30 seconds, synced speech and music, and up to 50 multimodal references. Here is how to drive it.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.0.text: Most video models think in five-second fragments; Seedance 2.5 thinks in scenes. It reasons about the entire take before rendering — so motion, lighting, and identity hold from first frame to last — and it generates synchronized speech, music, and effects natively. On ManifoldGen it runs as text-to-video, image-to-video, and a reference route that locks characters and sets across the whole clip.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.2.text: Prompt the arc, not the frame
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.3.text: Because the model plans whole-shot, describe what happens over time rather than composing one frozen moment:
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.5.text: Verbs carry sequence (sprints, vaults, lands, looks back), and the audio line gets its own beat ("heartbeat after she stops") that the model places correctly in time. That temporal awareness is the reason to pick 2.5 over fragment-based models for any shot with a beginning, middle, and end.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.7.text: The reference route accepts multiple images, videos, and audio clips as input. Feed it a character sheet, a set photo, or a brand product shot plus a prompt like "@Image1 is the barista, @Image2 is the café interior" and 2.5 holds both consistent across the take. This is the cheapest character-consistency workflow in the catalog — no training, no LoRA, just attachments.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.8.items.0: One reference per concept — a face sheet, a location plate, an object turntable.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.8.items.1: Say which is which in the prompt; do not make the model guess roles.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.8.items.2: Product shots: front-on hero image plus "rotate slowly around @Image1" beats re-prompting appearance every time.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.10.text: Native output is 480p and 720p. Draft at 480p where iteration cost is roughly half; finish at 720p for delivery or hand the chosen take to an upscaler. Audio quality is identical across tiers, so dialogue tests can always run cheap.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.11.title: Longer is not looser
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.11.text: Coherence comes from the whole-shot plan, but your prompt still needs one continuous idea per generation. A chase is a scene; a chase, then lunch, then a boardroom is three generations stitched.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.13.items.0: Middle of the clip drifts — your action list exceeds the duration budget. Cut actions or add seconds.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.13.items.1: Speech sounds rushed — allocate roughly two seconds per spoken clause and mark pauses with "then".
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.13.items.2: References bleed into each other — the model merged two faces. Use one clean frontal image per person and name them separately.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.13.items.3: Camera moves fight the choreography — give the camera its own sentence and keep it simple (one push-in, one follow).
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-2-5.blocks.14.text: Generate at /tools/seedance-2-5, animate a still at /tools/seedance-2-5-image, lock characters at /tools/seedance-2-5-reference — API mirrors under /api/video-generators/seedance-2-5.

/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.title: How to Use Seedance 4K for Native Ultra-HD Shots
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.excerpt: Seedance 4K runs Seedance 2.0 pinned to native ultra-HD output — one generation, no upscale pass. Here is when native pixels beat upscaling and how to art-direct for them.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.0.text: Most "4K AI video" is a 720p render stretched after the fact. Seedance 4K is different: it drives Seedance 2.0 straight into its native ultra-HD tier, so texture, edge detail, and on-screen text exist in the original pixels instead of being invented by a scaler. That costs more per second (from 747 credits for a 4-second clip) and buys the one thing upscalers cannot fake — real resolution where the camera looks.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.3.items.0: Hero shots that get cropped — 4K frames survive punch-ins and vertical reframes at full sharpness.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.3.items.1: Fine texture as subject — fabric weave, foliage, skin, water droplets. Upscalers average these; native rendering keeps them distinct.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.3.items.2: Ledger and signage — readable text in frame survives because the glyphs are rendered, not hallucinated by an upscale pass.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.3.items.3: Client delivery floors — broadcast and OOT specs that reject upscaled pipelines.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.4.text: And when it is not: anything destined for social feeds at 1080p or below. Draft those on Seedance 2 at one-fifth the rate and spend the difference on takes.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.6.text: Ultra-HD rewards prompts that name materials and optics. The model can only render detail you ask for:
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.8.text: Note the pattern: one precise action, then clauses about surface quality ("brushed", "screw slots", "micro-detail at the focal plane"), then restrained camera. In 4K every adjective renders — including ones you did not mean, like extra reflections from vague glass language.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.9.text: Keep durations short and shots tight
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.10.text: Native 4K generations are priced per second with no fast lane, so the economics favor short, dense shots: four seconds of hero material cut into a longer edit, not ten seconds of coverage. Storyboard first on cheaper tiers to lock timing, then re-run only the winning composition here.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.11.title: One hero per generation
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.11.text: Treat each 4K pass like film stock. Compose a single deliberate shot — macro insert, establishing aerial, product beauty — and let cheaper tiers handle connective tissue.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.13.items.0: Detail feels soft despite 4K — the prompt never named fine textures. Add material and optics language; resolution cannot invent unrequested detail.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.13.items.1: Costs ran away — you iterated composition at native rate. Lock framing on Seedance 2 first, then re-render the keeper.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.13.items.2: Shallow-focus backgrounds too busy — state the aperture intent ("f/1.8 look, background melts to bokeh").
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.13.items.3: Motion reads sluggish at macro distances — scale motion to lens length; macros need small real-world movement, not sweeps.
/blog/how-to-use-seedance-4k.blocks.14.text: Run it at /tools/seedance-4k, or automate through /api/video-generators/seedance-4k; draft the same prompts cheaply at /tools/seedance-2.

/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.title: How to Create AI Content for TikTok in 2026
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.excerpt: Generate AI video that performs on TikTok: vertical-native 9:16 prompts, a hook in the first second, seamless loops, and batch variation workflows.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.0.text: TikTok punishes landscape video twice: once when the letterboxed frame shrinks on the For You page, and again when the viewer has to rotate or squint. Generate vertical from the start — aspect 9:16 in every prompt — and compose for a phone held in one hand.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.1.text: This guide covers the four things that separate AI clips that travel from AI clips that die at 200 views: native vertical composition, a hook inside the first second, loop-ability, and batching enough variations to let the algorithm choose.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.3.items.0: Pick a satisfying subject. Macro food, textures, fluids, tools, cleaning, crafts. Subjects with continuous physical motion outperform narrative on a feed scrolled at one second per clip.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.3.items.1: Prompt natively vertical: state "9:16" intent through subject placement — tall glasses, standing figures, top-to-bottom pours. Center-weighted composition survives UI overlays.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.3.items.2: Front-load motion into the first second. The model spends early frames on your first clause, so open the prompt with the pour, the crack, the splash — not the setting.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.3.items.3: Design the loop: end state near start state. Ice settles back onto the glass rim; steam returns to stillness. A seamless loop multiplies watch time, and watch time is the metric.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.3.items.4: Batch 4–6 variations of the same prompt changing one variable each (backdrop color, camera distance, pour speed). Post the best performer; hold the rest as follow-ups.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.3.items.5: Post native resolution: 1080x1920, no watermark, caption and sound added in the app.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.5.example.label: Vertical macro hook
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.5.example.note: The action clause leads ("pouring into a tall glass") so frame one is already mid-motion — no establishing dead time. The tall glass fills the 9:16 frame naturally, and the swirl-to-settle arc reads as endless when looped.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.7.text: You have roughly one second before the swipe. That means the first frame must contain motion and the first half-second must escalate. Prompt structure controls this directly:
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.8.items.0: Open with the verb in motion: "pouring", "slicing", "spinning". Never "A quiet kitchen in the morning..." — that is a dead first frame.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.8.items.1: Name the payoff in the middle of the prompt where mid-clip frames land it: the crack, the reveal, the perfect swirl.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.8.items.2: "Slow motion" earns its place here: macro fluid dynamics are the rare subject where slowmo adds feed-stopping detail instead of dulling pace.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.8.items.3: Contrast carries thumbnails: bold flat backdrop colors (terracotta, cobalt, cream) make the moving subject pop even at stamp size.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.10.text: TikTok covers the right edge with engagement rail and the bottom third with caption and audio UI. Compose center-weighted: subject in the middle 60 percent of frame, critical detail slightly above center, nothing important hugging edges. In prompts this translates to simple geometry — "centered in frame", "tall glass filling the vertical frame", "shot straight on". Avoid prompts asking for wide environmental context; vertical plus busy edges guarantees your subject ends up behind a button.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.12.text: A seamless loop needs matching endpoints. Two reliable patterns:
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.13.items.0: Return to rest: the pour finishes, ice settles, surface stills. The last frame resembles the first. Say "seamless loop" explicitly; models trained on looping stock respond to it.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.13.items.1: Continuous cycle: stirring never stops, gears keep turning. Periodic motion hides the seam by construction. Add "constant speed" so the cycle does not decelerate at the clip boundary.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.15.title: Batch, do not perfect
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.15.text: TikTok rewards volume and lets the algorithm pick winners. Generate five variations of one concept in /studio, post the strongest, and repost variations days apart rather than polishing a single clip for hours. The winning variable is rarely the one you would have guessed.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.17.items.0: Clip feels dead in the feed — first frame is static. Reorder the prompt so the action clause comes first.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.17.items.1: Subject hidden behind UI — composition too wide or low. Recompose center-weighted, detail above center.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.17.items.2: Loop visibly jumps — end state differs from start. Switch to return-to-rest phrasing or constant-speed cyclic motion.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.17.items.3: Macro detail melts mid-clip — too many simultaneous motions. Cut to one primary motion plus one texture detail.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.17.items.4: Looks like an ad, gets skipped — drop "product lighting" for lifestyle subjects and re-add mixed ambient light per the realism pass.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.17.items.5: Vertical render crops oddly — the prompt described a horizontal scene. Rewrite around tall subjects: glasses, bottles, standing people, falling pours.
/blog/ai-content-for-tiktok.blocks.18.text: Draft three concepts tonight, run each as a 9:16 batch in /studio, and post the winner within 48 hours while you still care about the result. For lens and framing vocabulary to fill the skeleton with, see /tools/cinematic-cameras.

/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.title: How to Make Documentary Videos With AI in 2026
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.excerpt: Build documentary-style videos with AI the way editors actually work: stills first, Ken Burns motion second, archival looks, narration-first structure, honest labeling.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.0.text: Documentary is the one genre where AI video fails if you start with video. Long clips drift, faces mutate, and period detail dissolves after a few seconds. The workflow that holds up inverts the order: generate archival-quality stills, lock the look on those frames, then add restrained motion on top. You get the Ken Burns grammar audiences already accept from real documentaries, plus full control over every composition before anything moves.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.1.text: This guide walks the full pipeline — narration script, still generation, animation, and ethical labeling — using a real example: a 1930s shipyard sequence built from one generated press photograph. Everything runs in ManifoldGen; the prompts are copyable.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.3.items.0: Write the narration first. Documentary structure lives in the script: claim, evidence, scene. Cut the narration into beats of one or two sentences before generating anything.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.3.items.1: Cast each beat as a still. For every narration beat, write an image prompt in period-correct photographic language: era, subjects, setting, film stock. One beat, one frame.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.3.items.2: Generate and grade the stills until the visual world is consistent — same grain, same toning, same lens feel across every frame. Fix problems here, where regeneration costs seconds.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.3.items.3: Animate selectively. Only some stills deserve motion. Push-ins on faces, parallax on wide establishing shots, hold everything else as a true still.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.3.items.4: Label synthetic material. On-screen caption or end card stating AI-generated imagery. Non-negotiable for anything presented as history.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.4.text: Generate the archive still, then animate it
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.5.example.label: Archive still, then motion
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.5.example.note: The source still was generated with this image prompt: "Archival black-and-white photograph from the 1930s: shipyard workers in flat caps and overalls standing before an enormous half-built steel hull, scaffolding, overcast sky, film grain, slight sepia toning, documentary press photo." Because the motion prompt re-states the archival treatment (grain flicker, gate weave, sepia), the animated frames stay graded identically to the still instead of snapping to clean digital video.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.6.text: Two details make this read as archival rather than AI. First, "gate weave" — the tiny jitter of physical film in a projector — masks the micro-warping that gives synthetic video away. Second, the parallax clause adds depth without inventing geometry: scaffolding slides slightly against the hull while faces stay fixed.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.7.text: The archival look is a grade, not a filter word
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.8.text: "Vintage" alone returns modern footage with an orange tint. Period realism comes from stacking specific photographic facts that captions use:
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.9.items.0: Stock and process — "black-and-white with slight sepia toning" for pre-war, "Ektachrome, faded colors, dust and scratches" for mid-century color, "16mm, visible grain" for 1960s–70s reportage.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.9.items.1: Optics — "slightly soft focus", "vignetting at corners", "shallow vintage lens". Sharpness is the biggest tell of synthetic imagery.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.9.items.2: Damage vocabulary — "film grain", "dust specks", "gate weave", "light leak at frame edge". Pick two or three, not all of them.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.9.items.3: Composition conventions — press photos are eye-level, frontal, slightly imperfect framing. Ask for "documentary press photo" and let composition go candid.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.10.text: Apply the same grade words to both the still prompt and the motion prompt. The model animates toward its training distribution; restating the grade anchors the output there.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.12.text: Edit picture to the voiceover, never the reverse. A workable rhythm for a short piece: cold open on your strongest animated still (5 seconds), narration begins over a held photograph (8 seconds), push-in or parallax under the key claim, cut back to stills for supporting detail, end card with sources and the AI disclosure. Most beats should sit on static frames with only grain movement — motion loses authority when every shot moves.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.15.title: Motion serves memory, not spectacle
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.15.text: In documentary, animation exists to direct attention — toward a face, into a crowd, along a street. If a move does not point the viewer somewhere the narration names, leave the frame still. Restraint is what separates documentary from slideshow.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.17.items.0: Animated frames lose the film grade — the motion prompt omitted the treatment. Repeat the stock, toning, and damage words verbatim in the video prompt.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.17.items.1: Faces morph during push-in — the move is too fast or too long. Slow it, target a feature ("toward the workers' faces"), keep clips under 6 seconds.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.17.items.2: Parallax tears the scene apart — near and far elements are not clearly separated. Name two concrete layers, like scaffolding versus hull.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.17.items.3: Stills across scenes look inconsistent — regenerate from your best frame as the style anchor and reuse the identical grade phrase everywhere.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.17.items.4: Viewers assume it is real footage — your labeling is insufficient. Put the disclosure on screen during the footage, not only in the description.
/blog/documentary-videos-with-ai.blocks.18.text: Draft your script, cast its beats as stills, and test the strongest two as animated shots in Studio before committing to a full edit — the /tools/cinematic-cameras presets cover most of the push-in and parallax moves you will need.

/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.title: How to Turn a Photo Into an AI Video
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.excerpt: Turn any photo into a living AI video: pick source images that animate well, prompt motion that belongs to the scene, and keep identity perfectly stable.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.0.text: Image-to-video is the highest-leverage feature in AI video: one good photograph in, a few seconds of believable life out. It is also where most attempts fail, because people ask for motion the scene cannot support. A portrait does not need the camera to orbit — it needs an ear to twitch and the background bokeh to breathe. This guide covers choosing a source photo that animates cleanly, writing motion prompts that belong to the scene, and keeping the subject recognizably the same.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.1.text: The example below animates a single personal-style photo into a four-second clip. The same pipeline works for portraits, pets, product shots, and landscapes in ManifoldGen.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.2.text: Start with a photo built for motion
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.3.text: The model can only move what it can segment, so source quality decides more than your prompt does:
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.4.items.0: Sharp subject — eyes, fur, or edges in crisp focus. Motion amplifies softness into mush.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.4.items.1: Clean background separation — subject clearly distinct from backdrop. Busy scenes force the model to guess where the dog ends and the park begins.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.4.items.2: Single subject — one person or animal per frame. Two subjects trade identity mid-clip; groups are a different technique.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.4.items.3: Some motion already implied — wind-blown hair, string lights, water. The model extends existing energy far better than it invents new energy.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.4.items.4: Decent resolution — roughly 1024px on the long edge. Upscale first if not; animation cannot recover detail the source never had.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.5.text: Prompt motion that belongs to the scene
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.6.example.label: Personal photo, gentle motion
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.6.example.note: The source still was itself generated with this image prompt: "Candid smartphone photo of a golden retriever sitting on a picnic blanket in a park, tongue out, trees and bokeh string lights behind, late afternoon sun flare, slightly imperfect framing like a personal photo." Notice every motion clause names something already present in the frame — fur, grass, ears, lights, bokeh. Nothing asks the scene to gain a new element.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.7.text: Read that prompt as a checklist of ambient layers: environmental (breeze on fur and grass), expressive (head tilt toward camera), atmospheric (twinkling lights), optical (breathing bokeh), and camera (handheld micro-movement). One clause per layer, each tied to a visible element. That structure is why the result reads as a living moment instead of a morph.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.9.text: Identity drift — faces reshaping, markings migrating — is the failure mode people notice first. Three defenses:
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.10.items.0: Keep motion subtle by default. Every unit of movement is a chance to redraw the subject; "slightly", "gently", and "subtle" are load-bearing words, not filler.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.10.items.1: Never ask for pose changes beyond small ones. Head tilts, blinks, breaths, weight shifts work. Standing up, turning around, walking off do not.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.10.items.2: Use low strength when available. Lower image strength pins the output closer to the source pixels at the cost of less motion — the right trade for faces and pets.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.11.text: If the first generation drifts anyway, halve the number of motion clauses before touching anything else. Overloaded prompts make the model improvise.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.14.title: Animate what is already moving
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.14.text: The single rule behind every good image-to-video clip: extend motion that exists in the frame, never introduce motion that would require a new object, limb, or light source. Wind, blink, breathe, twinkle, ripple — then stop.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.16.items.0: Subject melts or changes species — too much requested motion. Cut to two clauses and add "subtle".
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.16.items.1: Clip looks like a static zoom — you described the camera but not the scene. Replace camera language with breeze, blink, and light clauses.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.16.items.2: New objects appear (extra dogs, floating leaves) — your prompt introduced elements absent from the photo. Describe only visible things.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.16.items.3: Motion starts strong then freezes — clip length exceeds the prompt's energy. Keep to 4 seconds or add one sustained ambient clause like "wind continues steadily".
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.16.items.4: Background warps badly — raise image strength / lower motion strength so the environment stays pinned while the subject moves.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.16.items.5: Face loses likeness across retries — regenerate from the original file each time, not from a previously animated frame.
/blog/turn-photo-into-ai-video.blocks.17.text: Pick three photos from your camera roll, run them through the skeleton above in Studio, and keep whichever clip earns a rewatch — then try the same source through different presets under /tools/cinematic-cameras to compare motion styles.

/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.title: How to Make AI Product Videos Without a Studio
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.excerpt: Skip the light table and crew: prompt AI product videos with precise material language, one hero move, controlled reflections, and seamless loops built for ads.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.0.text: A product video used to mean a light table, a macro rig, and a day of crew time. AI video replaces most of that — but only if you prompt like a cinematographer instead of a marketer. Commercial product footage has a grammar: the product described precisely enough to render its actual material, one hero move, reflections that look placed rather than accidental, and a loop clean enough to run as an ad. This guide gives you that grammar with a real generation.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.1.text: The example below is a four-second luxury loop of a perfume bottle — no camera, no studio, generated in ManifoldGen. The prompts are copyable.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.3.items.0: Write the product spec like a materials list. Material, finish, shape, color, surface state. "Black bottle" is nothing; "matte-black ceramic bottle" renders.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.3.items.1: Design the set. Pedestal or surface, backdrop, atmosphere. One surface, one backdrop gradient, at most one atmospheric element (mist, dust).
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.3.items.2: Choose one hero move. A slow rotate for bottles, a push-in for texture detail, a rise-and-reveal for packaging. One per clip.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.3.items.3: Direct the lighting explicitly. Name the source ("one large softbox") and its behavior ("sliding across the curved surface"). Reflections are your production value.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.3.items.4: Decide the destination before generating. Social placement wants 9:16; web hero loops want 16:9 or 1:1. Generate per placement rather than cropping.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.3.items.5: Generate short, judge the loop point, iterate on lighting words only once geometry is right.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.5.example.label: Hero loop
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.5.example.note: Every commercial decision is in one sentence: material (matte-black ceramic), stage (wet slate pedestal), backdrop (deep-charcoal gradient), lighting event (softbox reflection sliding), scale (macro lens), grade (luxury commercial), and edit intent (seamless loop). Nothing decorative competes with the rotate.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.6.text: "One large softbox reflection sliding across the curved surface" is what a gaffer produces with a real softbox on a move — a single elongated highlight traveling over the product as it turns. One named source with named behavior yields a coherent highlight instead of scattered specular noise.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.7.text: Describe the product like a materials list
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.8.text: Models know how finishes behave under light, but only if you name them:
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.9.items.0: Finish pairs with highlight behavior — matte absorbs (say "matte", "soft sheen"), gloss mirrors ("glossy", "mirror polish"), metal conducts ("brushed aluminum anisotropic streaks", "chrome with sharp reflections"), glass refracts ("thick glass, visible refraction through the liquid").
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.9.items.1: Shape needs geometry words — "cylindrical flacon", "faceted edges", "curved shoulder". Silhouettes drift without them.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.9.items.2: Surface state sells realism — "faint fingerprint-free surface", "condensation droplets" for cold drinks, "dust-free". Pick the state a stylist would create.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.9.items.3: Color gets a value — "deep-charcoal", "bone white". Bare color names render brighter than the physical object.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.11.text: Commercial lighting is few sources, precisely described. The vocabulary that works:
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.12.items.0: "One large softbox reflection" — the signature single-highlight look of premium tabletop work.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.12.items.1: "Soft deep-charcoal gradient backdrop" — separation plus depth with zero set dressing.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.12.items.2: "Rim light tracing the silhouette" — defines dark products against dark sets.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.12.items.3: "Luxury commercial lighting" / "high-end product photography lighting" — global grade terms worth one slot at the end.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.12.items.4: Atmosphere, singular — "thin mist drifting at the base" or "fine dust in the light beam". Two atmospherics fight each other.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.14.text: Ads live or die on the loop seam. Ask for it directly ("seamless loop"), keep the motion constant-speed, and end where you started: a full rotation back to the opening angle, or a push-in that settles on the exact first frame. Avoid one-directional moves — dolly-ins cannot loop; rotations can. Keep clips to 3–5 seconds so the seam arrives early.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.17.title: One move, one light story
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.17.text: A product clip fails when two things happen at once. If the bottle rotates, nothing else moves but mist and highlight. A push-in is a second clip for the same product; cutting two clips still beats one studio afternoon.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.19.items.0: Product shape mutates mid-rotate — the shape lacks geometry words. Add "cylindrical", "faceted", or "symmetrical" and slow the rotation.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.19.items.1: Label text warps — AI redraws typography every frame. Regenerate the product blank and overlay real label art in editing.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.19.items.2: Reflections flicker or scatter — more than one unnamed light. Cut back to "one large softbox" and delete competing light adjectives.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.19.items.3: Loop seam jumps — motion is not periodic. Switch to full rotation, or request "settles back on the opening frame".
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.19.items.4: Material looks plastic — finish is underspecified. Name the real material plus its highlight behavior ("brushed steel, anisotropic streaks").
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.19.items.5: Clip feels cheap despite good product — missing scale cue. Add "macro lens" and let shallow focus do the rest.
/blog/ai-product-videos-without-a-studio.blocks.20.text: Spec your product in one materials sentence, run the skeleton above at 4 seconds in Studio, then compare placements side by side using the the Studio presets before rendering final lengths.

/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.title: How to Make an AI Video From a Script in 2026
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.excerpt: Turn a written script into shot-by-shot AI video prompts: extract subject, action, camera, light, and ending per scene line and keep continuity across cuts.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.0.text: A script is already a prompt list — most people just hand it over whole. Video models generate one shot at a time, four or five seconds each. Feed them three pages of scene description and you get mush. Feed them one formatted line per shot and the edit assembles itself.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.1.text: This guide walks through converting a two-scene script into two prompts, generating both clips with ManifoldGen, and cutting them together into a coherent sequence. The workflow scales to any length: every scene heading becomes one or more shot prompts, never more than one shot per prompt.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.2.text: The workflow: script line to shot prompt
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.3.items.0: Break the script into shots. Each EXT./INT. scene line is at least one shot; action lines with their own camera logic become additional shots. A 60-second piece is typically 12–16 four-second clips.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.3.items.1: Extract five fields from each scene line: subject, action, camera move, lighting, ending state. If a field is missing from the script, invent it once and lock it — that decision now belongs to the world.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.3.items.2: Write one prompt per shot using the skeleton below. Camera clause directly after the subject, exactly as you would for any directed shot.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.3.items.3: Repeat world details across prompts verbatim. Same palette words ("cold blue-grey"), same weather ("sheets of rain"), same time of day in every shot of the sequence. Continuity lives in repeated adjectives.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.3.items.4: Generate at low duration first, review all shots together on a timeline, regenerate only the weak ones.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.3.items.5: Cut in an editor: trim each clip to its strongest 2.5–3.5 seconds, order follows the script, no transitions. Hard cuts are the grammar.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.5.text: Here is the entire source material — a standard scene breakdown:
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.7.text: Two scene headings, two establishing details, two actions. That maps cleanly to two prompts.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.9.example.label: Scene 1 — EXT. STORM CLIFF – NIGHT
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.9.example.note: This shot carries the scene heading itself: exterior, night, weather, scale. The wide aerial push establishes geography before any close-up exists, which is what an establishing shot is for — and "toward the lantern room" aims the move at where Scene 2 will take us.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.10.example.label: Scene 2 — INT. LAMP ROOM – NIGHT
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.10.example.note: The INT. heading becomes a close-up interior with shallow depth of field — the contrast with Shot 1 does the storytelling. Rain-streaked glass and cold blue night repeat Scene 1's weather and palette verbatim, so the cut reads as the same world minutes apart.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.12.text: Models have no memory between generations. The only continuity mechanism you control is word-for-word repetition across prompts. Pick a small vocabulary per project and reuse it mechanically:
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.13.items.0: Palette: name two or three colors once ("cold blue-grey", "warm amber") and use them in every shot.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.13.items.1: Weather and time: "night", "sheets of rain" appear in both prompts above. Drop them and the second clip silently becomes a different evening.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.13.items.2: Recurring objects: if the lighthouse beam matters, it appears in the exterior and as moving light inside the interior. Same object, different angle.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.13.items.3: Style anchor: one phrase like "dramatic documentary energy" in every prompt keeps grade and texture consistent even when subjects change.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.15.text: Plan on 4-second renders even when your edit needs longer takes. Short clips generate faster, fail cheaper, and force the discipline of one idea per shot. In the timeline, trim each clip to its best 2.5–3.5 seconds so motion never visibly loops or stalls at the edges. Cut on action — hands turning a wheel, waves mid-explosion — and the seams disappear. For pacing reference, dialogue-free sequences like this one sit comfortably at one cut every 2–4 seconds.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.17.title: One shot per prompt
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.17.text: Never ask a single generation to cover a whole scene. A prompt describing the lighthouse, then the interior, then the keeper walking upstairs produces a morphing compromise. Each scene heading yields its own prompt; each prompt yields one composition, one move, one action.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.19.items.0: Shots look like different worlds — a detail changed between prompts. Audit palette, weather, and time-of-day words; they must match character-for-character.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.19.items.1: Clip contains two locations — the prompt covered more than one shot. Split it at the scene heading and generate again.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.19.items.2: Interior feels disconnected from exterior — the establishing shot named no destination. End exteriors with a move toward whatever the next interior shows.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.19.items.3: Sequence feels flat — every shot uses the same size. Alternate wide establishing shots with close-ups the way the script alternates EXT/INT.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.19.items.4: Motion stalls before the cut ends — no ending state defined. Add a settle clause ("settles on the rotating lens") so the last frames hold a stable frame.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-from-script.blocks.20.text: Draft your scene breakdown, convert each heading with the skeleton, and run the shots side by side in /studio before committing to final renders. For camera-move vocabulary to fill the skeleton with, see /tools/cinematic-cameras.

/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.title: How to Make AI Video Look Real in 2026
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.excerpt: Realism in AI video comes from imperfection and light physics: handheld shake, mixed color temps, natural exposure, mundane action. Exact prompt language inside.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.0.text: AI video looks fake for one reason: it is too perfect. Frames are clean, motion is smooth, lighting is flattering, and every shot is composed like a poster. Real footage — the footage models were trained on — is handheld, slightly miss-framed, lit by whatever bulbs were in the room, and mostly shows people doing boring things.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.1.text: So the technique is subtraction plus physics. Remove every "cinematic" word from your vocabulary, then describe how light actually behaves and how an actual camera actually fails. Two passes on real generations below show exactly what that looks like.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.3.items.0: Camera: "handheld smartphone footage" or "static tripod shot" with "slight camera shake". Never "sweeping", "epic", or "dynamic".
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.3.items.1: Framing: "imperfect framing", "off-center", "partially blocked by a passerby". Real cameras miss.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.3.items.2: Color: "mixed daylight and tungsten", "natural color", "unstylized". Mixed color temperature is the single strongest realism signal.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.3.items.3: Exposure: "natural exposure", "soft highlight rolloff", no HDR words. Blown window highlights are honest; perfect dynamic range is not.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.3.items.4: Texture: "subtle sensor noise" mimics the compression grain of training data. Clean pixels read as CGI.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.3.items.5: Action: mundane and single. Pouring, sorting, wiping, waiting. Nobody backflips through a fish market.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.3.items.6: Grade: never say cinematic, dramatic (unless documentary-dramatic), 8K, hyperrealistic, or masterpiece. Each one pushes the model toward its most saturated, overproduced output.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.5.example.label: Imperfection pass
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.5.example.note: Every clause attacks one tell of synthetic footage: shake kills glide, imperfect framing kills poster composition, mixed bulbs kill the graded look, "documentary realism" anchors the whole style. The subject is deliberately ordinary — ice, fish, steam.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.7.example.label: Light-physics pass
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.7.example.note: "Nothing dramatic happens" is a deliberate constraint, not a joke. It forbids the model from inventing events, so the clip spends its entire budget on believable micro-motion: drifting dust, curling steam. Volumetric details like dust motes in a hard shaft also prove the light source has a direction.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.8.text: Light-physics phrases worth memorizing: "dust motes in window light", "soft highlight rolloff", "light falls off across the room", "practicals visible in frame" (lamps and ceiling fixtures that justify the illumination), "shadows fall left of frame". Any one of these does more for believability than ten style adjectives, because they force consistent geometry between light source, shadow, and surface.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.9.text: What to delete from your prompts
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.10.items.0: "Cinematic" — triggers teal-orange grading and shallow-everything focus.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.10.items.1: "Hyperrealistic / ultra detailed / 8K" — pushes toward rendered, plastic textures, the opposite of the goal.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.10.items.2: "Beautiful woman / handsome man" — faces drift toward airbrushed stock. Describe clothing, age, and activity instead.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.10.items.3: "Slow motion" everywhere — reserve it for genuine high-speed subjects; as a default it makes walking look underwater.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.10.items.4: "Perfect symmetry, centered composition" — real footage is off-balance. Ask for the opposite.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.12.title: Boring is believable
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.12.text: The fastest route to realistic AI video is a subject nobody would film beautifully. A vendor tossing ice beats a warrior drawing a sword every time, because the model has millions of shaky phone clips of markets and none of choreographed sword fights. Pick subjects from life, describe them plainly, and let imperfection do the styling.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.14.items.0: Still looks like CGI — remove all remaining style adjectives and add "shot on a phone" plus a mixed-lighting source.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.14.items.1: Motion is unnaturally smooth — the camera clause got buried. Put "handheld" first and delete competing movement words.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.14.items.2: Colors look graded despite "natural color" — another phrase is overriding it, usually "cinematic" or "golden" outside golden hour. Strip them.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.14.items.3: Faces uncanny — keep faces small in frame, backlit, or in profile; close front-lit faces expose skin rendering first.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.14.items.4: Too much happening — you listed three actions. One action, one background detail, nothing else.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.14.items.5: Noise looks like artifacting — reduce to "subtle sensor noise"; heavy grain words degrade fine detail instead of adding texture.
/blog/how-to-make-ai-video-look-real.blocks.15.text: Take any prompt you already have, strip the style words, run it through the skeleton above, and compare both clips in /studio. For focal-length language that keeps perspective honest, pair this with /tools/cinematic-cameras.

/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.title: How to Start a Faceless Channel With AI
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.excerpt: A faceless channel is an asset pipeline: pick a repeatable niche, generate voiceover and b-roll in batches, build loops that monetize, ship on a calendar.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.0.text: A faceless channel is not a channel without you on camera; it is a channel where every asset is replaceable. Voiceover, b-roll, music, thumbnail — none of it depends on your presence, which means all of it can be generated, batched, and scheduled. That is the entire advantage: you compete on consistency of output, not charisma.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.1.text: This guide walks through niche selection, a three-asset pipeline (voiceover plus generated visuals plus music), a batching workflow for a weekly calendar, and the format decisions per platform — vertical for Shorts and TikTok, 16:9 for YouTube long-form. You need a video generation tool such as /studio, a voiceover tool, and two to three hours per week.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.2.text: Pick a niche you can template
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.3.text: Faceless channels die from variety, not competition. Every format change forces new prompts, new pacing, new research. Choose a niche where one visual recipe repeats forever:
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.4.items.0: Ambience — rain rooms, fireplaces, study scenes. The visual is a single slow loop; monetization comes from watch time on multi-hour uploads built from repeated loops.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.4.items.1: History — narrated events over period-style b-roll. One documentary structure, endless subjects.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.4.items.2: Finance explainers — charts, city footage, abstract motion under tight scripts. High CPM, low visual risk.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.4.items.3: Sci-fi stories — original micro-fiction over generated alien landscapes and characters. Highest ceiling, hardest consistency problem.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.5.text: Test a niche by writing ten titles first. If ten strong titles do not come easily in twenty minutes, the niche will starve. If they come easily, write the recurring shot list next — most niches settle into five to eight reusable scene types that cover ninety percent of episodes.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.7.items.0: Script first, always. 150 spoken words per minute of runtime. Write the full script before generating anything so visuals serve narration instead of replacing it.
/blog/start-faceless-channel-with-ai.blocks.7.items.1: Voiceover. Generate the complete narration track, then cut it into segments at natural pauses. Segment timestamps become your edit skeleton.
